# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# A careful reading of the Varden and Halden 24-month follow-up

**Bottom line:** This is a strong follow-up. It answers the open questions from earlier reports and corrects both previous overreaches: Varga and Holm's "entirely an artifact" and the meta-analysis's "no sign of decay". Its numbers are consistent. But it has three weaknesses the authors don't fully deal with:

- The control arm was **contaminated**, which affects how much the gain really faded.
- The new **log-based hours measure** is a different construct from timesheet hours, not simply a stricter one.
- The mediation result is described as "confirmed", which the analysis cannot support.

## 1. The arithmetic checks out

- **Timesheets:** 0.966 / 0.88 ≈ 1.098, so +9.8%.
- **System logs:** 0.966 / 0.89 ≈ 1.085, so +8.5%.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, a 13.4% fall in hours. 96.8 / 0.866 ≈ 1.118, so +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares** sum to 100% (47 + 18 + 35), and both intervals are symmetric.
- **Meetings:** treated offices fell by 3.5 hours and control offices by 0.2, a difference of 3.3. That matches the 3.3-hour gap at month six.
- **The counter arm's 12% extra staff** is consistent with the 9-month result. With output per employee down 11.4%, restoring output needs 1 / 0.886 ≈ 1.13 times the staff.

## 2. What it gets right

- **The mediation analysis was registered before 24-month outcomes were available**, as Varga and Holm demanded.
- **A second hours measure was added** to address the worry about unrecorded work.
- **The study meets the standards Varga and Holm set themselves**: record-based output, measured hours, randomisation and two-year follow-up. On that basis it fairly rejects their "entirely an artifact" claim.
- **It checked the meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies.** All four were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which is exactly the problem I raised with the meta-analysis's duration analysis.
- **The Halden subset is honestly described** as "survivors twice over" and an upper bound.
- **The unplanned meeting-audit observation is suitably hedged.** The authors also correctly note that the trial cannot tell whether reorganising without cutting hours would capture the gain.
- **Ending the counter arm, with its cost estimate**, is a useful real-world result in its own right.

## 3. Control contamination affects the "fading" estimate

In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their meetings and their output per hour rose 4.1%. The authors treat this as a separate observation, but it feeds directly into the main estimate.

- **It inflates the control group.** Two of seven offices gaining about 4.1% raises the control average by roughly 1.2 points for months 15 to 24.
- **That shrinks the treated-control gap.** The like-for-like decline was from 12.5% to 9.8%, or 2.7 points. **Perhaps around 1.2 points of that is control improvement, not treated offices fading.**
- **So the authors' statement in section 5 that the gain "declined by about a quarter" is overstated.** The two intervals overlap substantially anyway (+6.9% to +18.4% against +4.6% to +15.2%), so the decline is not statistically established.
- **It may also be spillover.** Office-level randomisation was chosen to prevent contamination. Control offices adopting the treated offices' main practice is the kind of spillover it was meant to stop.
- **The control meeting figures need checking.** If two control offices fell by about 2.1 hours each, the control average falling only 0.2 hours (7.2 to 7.0) means the other five rose by about 0.5 hours each. That may be real meeting creep, or a sign that the 7.1 figure is measured at month 15 rather than baseline. It should be clarified.

None of this weakens the persistence finding. If anything, the treated offices' effect against an uncontaminated control would be larger and fade less than reported.

## 4. Log-in time measures something different

The authors call log-measured hours the "stricter measure", but they measure something else:

- **They capture only on-system work.** Unclaimed work done off the system, such as reading, email, phone calls or thinking at home, is still missed. The concern about unrecorded work is only partly addressed.
- **They count time logged in, not time working.** "Active" log-in time may still include idle time.
- **This changes what the meetings result means.** If log time excludes meetings, the 8.5% is output per hour of case work. Cutting meetings can't raise that by freeing up time. It would have to work by reducing fragmentation and interruptions, which is a different mechanism from simply removing unproductive hours.
- **On timesheet hours, meetings could explain far more.** Removing meeting time:

| | Timesheet hours | Meeting hours | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | ~37.9 | 7.0 | ~30.9 |
| Treated | ~33.4 | 3.9 | ~29.5 |

Non-meeting hours fell about 5%, and output per employee fell 3.4%. On this measure, cutting meetings could account for most of the gain. So the 47% share depends heavily on which hours measure is used. That's worth stating explicitly.

## 5. The mediation result is overstated in the summary

- **"Confirms" is too strong.** The limitations section says mediation "assumes no unmeasured confounding". Meeting cuts were managers' choices, not randomised, so better managers could cause both fewer meetings and higher productivity.
- **There are still only 14 clusters.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds repeated observations of the same offices, not independent ones. The intervals depend on a small-cluster correction, and none is mentioned (the same issue as in the 9-month report).
- **Some of the data may have been seen before.** The hypothesis came from month-six data. If the registered analysis pools office-months from the whole trial, it partly reuses the data that suggested it. The report should say which months the mediation model uses.
- **The meeting baseline is new.** The 9-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six, but this report gives baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2). These were presumably taken retrospectively from calendars, which should be stated. They do resolve my earlier concern about a pre-existing imbalance, since the arms look balanced at baseline.

A fair summary: **the meetings pathway passed a registered test and is the leading candidate mechanism, but has not been shown to be causal.**

## 6. Questions left open in Varden

- **Backlogs and deadlines are still not reported.** The 9-month report named backlogs breaching statutory deadlines as the key 24-month risk, and output measured as cases closed could hide them. Backlog size, case age and deadline compliance should be in Table 1.
- **Case-processing costs are not reported.** The authors estimated cost per contact for the counter arm but give no cost per case for case-processing, which includes paid overtime.
- **Quality figures are still levels, not difference-in-differences.** The overturn rate of 3.2% against 3.0% has no interval.

## 7. Questions about the Halden follow-up

- **Response bias.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded. The nine that didn't may include more reversions or poorer results.
- **One reversion is reclassified to fit the narrative.** The summary says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations". But the marketing agency cited **client deadlines**, which the meta-analysis's own definition puts under *discretionary* work. That is a discretionary-work reversion. It suggests deadline-heavy discretionary roles can fail too, which refines the "presence-dependent" distinction rather than confirming it.
- **Attrition is not addressed.** Okafor, an author of the original Halden paper, is a co-author here. The report doesn't correct or acknowledge the misreported withdrawals that Varga and Holm found. This isn't evidence of bias in this report, but the record should be corrected.
- **The baseline is two years old.** Comparing with the pre-pilot baseline more than two years later picks up economic changes too.

## 8. Where the evidence stands after five documents

| Question | Current best reading |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | **About 8–10%, persisting to 24 months** in the only randomised long-term study. Possibly larger against an uncontaminated control |
| Output per employee, discretionary | **Slightly lower, about 2–4%**, mostly but not fully offset |
| Coverage-bound work | **Not viable without extra staff.** The Varden arm was ended; about 12% more staff and 9% higher cost per contact would be needed |
| Fading | **Possibly modest**, but partly confounded by control contamination. Not to zero |
| Mechanism | **Meetings look like the main pathway, fatigue a smaller one, about a third unexplained.** Not shown to be causal |
| Reorganisation without cutting hours | **Untested.** Two-office hint only |
| "Sector-general" / "entirely artifact" / "no decay" | **All three rejected** |
| Generalisability | One public employer, 14 clusters; the private-sector evidence is uncontrolled |

**The key next study** is a three-arm trial: reduced hours, reorganisation (such as a meeting audit) with unchanged hours, and control. It should measure output from records, track both total and on-system hours, report backlogs and costs, and use small-cluster-robust inference. The meeting audit in the control offices suggests the reorganisation-only arm is the most important unknown in this literature.
